newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS - Norilsk plans rights issue, shares slump.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Norilsk plans rights issue, shares slump.

text.p: Russia's troubled mining and metals mammoth RAO Norilsky Nikel said on Tuesday it planned to double its capital through a rights issue, sending shares plunging on the Russian Trading System.
The news, coming in the midst of the sale of a controlling stake in the company, added further confusion to the already muddied final phase of Russia's privatisation programme.

Norilsk said it would propose issuing around 126 million ordinary shares to existing shareholders at a price of 30,000 roubles each. Shareholders will vote on the proposals at an extraordinary meeting set for September 8.
If approved, the issue would raise around $650 million for the debt-ridden company, one of the world's largest producers of nickel and precious metals.
But the 30,000 rouble price tag, which at Tuesday's exchange rate is $5.17, is well below Tuesday's closing ordinary share price of $14.00.
Traders' concern that new shares would end up on the market once shareholders had bought them up in the rights issue sent Norilsk shares spiralling 17 percent lower from Monday's close of $17.00.
"The shares are down on the issue news. People perceive that there will be some kind of value dilution through such an issue," said one Russian dealer.
With the issue priced at such a heavy discount to current market values, further price falls should not be ruled out, another dealer said.
Preferred Norilsk shares finished the day slightly higher at $12.70 from $12.00 at the close on Monday.

Norilsk spokesman Anatoly Komrakov declined to speculate on what the issue and the proposed pricing might mean for share prices, or why the shares were being valued at 30,000 roubles. They have a nominal value of 250 roubles.
"Our auditors said that it was necessary to issue these shares to further develop our group and to attract investment," he said.
It was also unclear how the issue would affect a tender for a 38 percent stake, representing 51 percent of voting shares, in the Norilsk group, which opened last week and closes on Friday.
The winner of the sale is due to be announced on August 5.
One dealer said those bidding in the tender were likely to have been aware of the proposals before entering the running.
"On this kind of thing the bidders would have been informed beforehand. I think the proposals will have met with their approval first," he said.
The winner of the investment tender would have to increase its stake significantly to hold on to a voting majority if the issue is approved.

Norilsk currently has authorised capital of about 126 million shares made up of 94.5 million ordinary and 31.5 million preferred. The issue would significantly change the balance between ordinary and preferred shares.

Traders said the issue announcement is unlikely to affect the outcome of the tender, which Russian traders and analysts widely expect to go to commercial bank Uneximbank. The bank had control of the stake under a government shares-for-loans scheme.
The Russian government and privatisation officials have so far failed to clarify whether the Norilsk tender is open to foreign participation.

Uneximbank maintains foreign companies are not allowed to bid for such a large stake in a company considered to be of strategic importance to the country, while the Federal Property Fund said it was unaware of any restrictions on foreigners.
Norilsk shares were particularly vulnerable to a sharp sell-off on Tuesday having risen so strongly in recent days, traders said. Ordinary shares were trading below $12.00 earlier this month.
"The shares must look vulnerable simply because...they have gone up significantly fairly recently," Martin Diggle, director at Brunswick brokerage, said.
